assessmentSummary.identity: One Big Toe Press Iso Hold repetition is performed on one target foot. Start with the target heel, first and fifth metatarsal heads, relaxed hallux, and lesser toes supported on a clean dry level surface. Press the hallux plantarward into the surface to a comfortable prescribed submaximal effort without curling the lesser toes, lifting the heel or metatarsal heads, rolling the foot, or turning the task into an arch dome. Maintain the timed isometric press while breathing, then reduce pressure with control until the hallux returns to the same relaxed supported start. Record left and right repetitions and actual hold seconds separately. Standing hands-free, standing light wall-touch, and seated stable-bench support are exact variants. A press-and-lift sequence, lesser-toe action, toe yoga, short-foot doming, toe curl, dynamic repetitions, manual assistance, resistance, unstable or single-leg support, maximal force testing, or clinical treatment changes the variant or definition.
currentCardFindings: Source 848 has a stable legacy definition but its only variant lacks exact target-foot setup, hallux-only action, full release endpoint, side count, support options, anatomy, load, fatigue, duration, relationship, and review contracts.
The identity is a submaximal sustained hallux plantarflexion press. Maximal laboratory contractions are adjacent evidence and are not adopted as a workout target.
All five legacy YouTube candidates returned healthy oEmbed metadata, but no candidate has been watched, mapped to an exact variant, checked for captions or safety, or approved.
assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Select only when the exact support variant, target side, foot-safe surface, hallux and forefoot contact, comfortable submaximal press, symptoms, restrictions, dose, duration, and cumulative toe, foot, calf, balance, running, landing, jumping, agility, and lower-body budgets fit. Do not silently change the hallux action, lesser-toe behavior, support, assistance, resistance, contraction mode, effort target, count, or clinical scope. Recompute logistics, duration, fatigue, substitutions, persistence, and coach and athlete rendering after every change.

calibrationEvidence.basis: Direct hallux-flexion task descriptions, hallux plantarflexion conditioning research, hallux-contact limits-of-stability research, short-foot and intrinsic-foot task mechanics, general supervised-exercise safeguards, Source 848 context, five oEmbed records, and comparison with Toe Yoga, Short-Foot Drill, Foot Tripod Weight Shifts, toe flexion, and compound heel raising.
calibrationEvidence.uncertainty: Research does not validate one universal effort, hold, support position, dose, frequency, fatigue ceiling, recovery interval, outcome, or Vortex score. Maximal contractions and clinical study protocols are not universal workout prescriptions. No media, relationship, or score has human approval.

currentCardSnapshot.description: With one target foot supported on a clean dry level surface, press the hallux gently into the floor to the prescribed comfortable submaximal effort. Keep the heel and first and fifth metatarsal heads down, keep lesser toes relaxed, hold while breathing, then reduce pressure with control until the hallux returns to the same supported start. Record left and right repetitions and hold seconds separately. Standing hands-free, standing light wall-touch, and seated stable-bench support are exact variants.

environment.surface: clean dry level stable nonslip foot-safe floor
environment.space: one visible seated or standing foot-control station with clear entry and exit
environment.hygiene: follow facility foot-contact and shared-station policy
environment.coachSightline: top and front-quarter views of hallux, lesser toes, metatarsal heads, heel, arch, ankle, support, breathing, and symptoms
environment.changeRule: A change to target digit group, support, assistance, resistance, contraction mode, dose, symptoms, or downstream demand requires revalidation.

selectionPrerequisites: safe visible station and exact selected support
comfortable hallux and forefoot contact without symptom provocation
understands hallux press, lesser-toe relaxation, hold, release, side-specific count, stop signal, and exit
same-session toe, foot, calf, balance, and lower-body budgets fit
excludeOrEscalate: current symptom, restriction, trauma, procedure, skin issue, circulation, or neurologic concern conflicting with exact task
sharp or increasing pain, persistent cramp, new numbness, tingling, weakness, circulation or skin change
dizziness, faintness, chest pain, unusual breathlessness, disorientation, or inability to communicate
unsafe surface, hygiene, visibility, bench, wall, space, communication, or exit
notEstablishedByEvidence: universal effort, hold, dose, frequency, recovery, or outcome
diagnosis, treatment, clearance, maximal assessment, or isolated-muscle claim

evidence.sourceTitle: The influence of body posture and added mass on intrinsic and extrinsic foot muscle activation and force output during common foot strengthening exercises
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Foot and Ankle Research
claims: The study instructed hallux flexion toward the ground as a distinct task.
Vortex defines a target-foot submaximal press, prescribed isometric hold, controlled release, and side-specific count.

evidence.sourceTitle: Clarification of functional differences between the hallux and lesser toes during the single leg stance: immediate effects of conditioning contraction of the toe plantar flexion muscles
claims: Hallux plantar-flexion contractions and lesser-toe contractions were treated separately.
The card separates hallux press from toe yoga, toe curling, short-foot doming, and whole-foot weight shifting.

evidence.sourceTitle: The influence of body posture and added mass on intrinsic and extrinsic foot muscle activation and force output during common foot strengthening exercises
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Foot and Ankle Research
claims: Hallux-flexion tasks were assessed with intrinsic and extrinsic foot muscle measures.
The card names contributors, joints, action, planes, contacts, and laterality without claiming isolation.

evidence.sourceTitle: Clarification of functional differences between the hallux and lesser toes during the single leg stance: immediate effects of conditioning contraction of the toe plantar flexion muscles
claims: The study used a standing hallux plantar-flexion isometric contraction with plantar-pressure feedback.
Vortex uses a submaximal floor press with no required feedback and rejects lesser-toe curl, heel lift, forefoot lift, foot roll, and missing release.

evidence.sourceTitle: The influence of body posture and added mass on intrinsic and extrinsic foot muscle activation and force output during common foot strengthening exercises
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Foot and Ankle Research
claims: Task posture changes muscle activation and force behavior in common foot exercises.
Candidate scores describe exercise complexity and physical demand only; they do not classify people.

evidence.sourceTitle: Clarification of functional differences between the hallux and lesser toes during the single leg stance: immediate effects of conditioning contraction of the toe plantar flexion muscles
claims: The study used brief maximal conditioning contractions, not a universal training dose.
Vortex tracks actual hold seconds, effort, support, side, faults, symptoms, and overlapping toe and foot exposure rather than treating research testing as a recovery prescription.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Safe exercise delivery requires appropriate instruction, environment, progression, and supervision.
Vortex requires a clean dry level surface, toe visibility, selected support, hygiene, communication, space, and exit conditions without demographic classification.

evidence.sourceTitle: Clarification of functional differences between the hallux and lesser toes during the single leg stance: immediate effects of conditioning contraction of the toe plantar flexion muscles
claims: The study's six-second maximal contraction was an experimental conditioning protocol.
Candidate comfortable holds and repetition ranges remain quarantined and stop before contacts, toe relaxation, body control, or symptom quality degrades.

evidence.sourceTitle: The influence of body posture and added mass on intrinsic and extrinsic foot muscle activation and force output during common foot strengthening exercises
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Foot and Ankle Research
claims: A direct hallux-flexion instruction is to flex the big toe toward the ground.
Vortex adds supported start, lesser-toe relaxation, submaximal hold, full release, side count, and observable faults.

evidence.sourceTitle: Noncontact of the unilateral hallux with the ground reduces forward limits of stability while standing
claims: Hallux ground contact influenced forward limits of stability in the study.
Stop for pain, neurologic or skin signs, lost contacts, toe cramp, unsafe setup, loss of control, or participant request; do not force a press.

evidence.sourceTitle: Evidence for Intrinsic Foot Muscle Training in Improving Foot Function: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
claims: Intrinsic-foot programs vary in exercise selection, dose, and outcomes.
The hold may be selected for preparation or resilience only when purpose and cumulative foot and toe budgets fit; no universal outcome is promised.

evidence.sourceTitle: Clarification of functional differences between the hallux and lesser toes during the single leg stance: immediate effects of conditioning contraction of the toe plantar flexion muscles
claims: The experimental task distinguished hallux from lesser-toe plantar-flexion effort.
Athlete support uses one big toe, a gentle press, quiet lesser toes, breathing, full release, and a stop-before-cramp rule.

evidence.sourceTitle: The influence of body posture and added mass on intrinsic and extrinsic foot muscle activation and force output during common foot strengthening exercises
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Foot and Ankle Research
claims: Hallux flexion is a separately described common foot task.
Coaches record target side, support, hallux contact, lesser-toe curl, heel or metatarsal lift, foot roll, hold, release, first fault, symptoms, and actual exposure without diagnosing impairment.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Exercise selection and progression should fit the actual task, setting, and supervision.
Wall-touch or seated support, smaller effort, shorter holds, fewer repetitions, more rest, captions, transcript, stills, and clear side markers can improve access while preserving identity.

evidence.sourceTitle: Intrinsic Foot Muscle Activation During Specific Exercises: A T2 Time Magnetic Resonance Imaging Study
claims: Specific short-foot and selective-toe tasks are distinct exercises with different activation protocols.
Hallux pressing, selective extension, toe spreading, toe curling, short-foot doming, pressure shifting, and heel raising retain explicit boundaries.
